Replace.Text: Gold gets a market. Borrow from other civilizations or a bond market, lend to a neighbour who's short, set your taxes with a policy card, and let an auto-loan guard keep you clear of the game's negative-balance penalties; a missed payment or a repudiated debt costs you your good name. Resources get world prices, trading partners settle what they owe each other every turn, and you can put a tariff on a partner or invest in a neighbour's builds and treasury. Wars, disasters and debt push the world through booms and slumps, inflation can push prices up, old markets and banks fade across the ages, and your government sets how your economy runs. The computer players play by the same rules. Single-player.
Whether civilizations can borrow from each other and, later, from a bond market, within a limit set by income. Off turns the loans off; trade bills and investment keep their own options.
Nobody borrows or lends, and the guard stays out.
Loans between civilizations open with Moneylending, the bond market with Public debt.

When your treasury is about to go below zero while your income is at or below zero, the guard takes out an emergency loan for you, up to a cap of ten turns of your income. Past that your overdraft takes over. You can also switch it on the Loans tab.
You borrow only when you ask to. The game's penalties for a negative balance apply as usual.
An emergency loan covers a shortfall before the game's penalties start, until the cap is reached. You're told once when it is.

Whether the computer players use Economics' systems by its rules: borrowing and lending, restructuring and repudiating, investment and aid, tariffs, crisis responses and bankruptcy. Off, the world still charges them as it does you, and their choices are left to the game's own AI.
Only you borrow and lend. The computer players keep their treasuries as the base game runs them.

The rate every loan starts from: 1.5 percent a turn in Antiquity, 1 in Exploration and 0.75 in Modern at Standard. Each loan's actual rate then moves with the borrower's payment record, its relationship with the lender, its banking buildings and the world economy. The rate cap scales with it.

[B]The business cycle[/B][N]The world's economy runs on one index. It reads 1.00 when the world is steady. Events move it: wars, captured and razed settlements, disasters, defaults and repudiated debts pull it down; peace, new trade routes, income growing faster than usual and easy credit push it up. Left alone it drifts back toward 1.00 by a tenth of the gap each turn.[N][N][B]The bands[/B][N]Below 0.80 a Depression. 0.80 to 0.95 a Slump. 0.95 to 1.05 Steady. Above 1.05 a Boom. A Panic is a state of its own: too much credit in a Boom drops the index by 0.20, freezes the lenders and lasts 5 turns.[N][N][B]The needle[/B][N]Your own economy, {1_Mine} ({2_MinePhase}): the world's index, {3_World} ({4_WorldPhase}), plus how the events you took part in moved you.[N][N][B]What it does to you[/B][N]{5_Effect} The bond market's rate rises as the index falls and eases as it climbs. When the civilizations with Public debt owe the bond market a lot beside the Gold they hold, their prices climb a little every turn: everything they buy with Gold costs more, for the computer players as for you, and bond loans get dearer. Prices start over with each age. Off by default.
Bond debt pushes up what everything costs to buy and raises bond rates.

Wars, captures, disasters, the age's crisis, defaults and changes in trade move a world economic index and each civilization's own economy through booms and slumps. A boom pays Gold each turn and makes bonds cheaper; a slump takes Gold and makes them dearer. This sets how hard each event and each Panic hits; Economic swings sets how far the economy runs.
Events and Panics move the economy half as much.
Events move the economy by their full weight.
Events and Panics move the economy half again as much.
How far booms and slumps run. With momentum, a downturn feeds on itself and a boom overshoots when it turns, so the same war can blow over in one game and become a depression in another.
The economy drifts back to normal quickly. A deep slump costs a few percent of your income.
Booms and busts build on themselves. A depression can take a third to half of your income for a few turns, about as much as an age's crisis, and a boom can add a quarter.
Wilder still: booms run higher, busts fall further and both last longer.

Each civilization's government, or its ideology in the Modern age, sets how its economy runs: Despotism lives on tribute, a Classical Republic borrows from its citizens, Communism plans production, and more. The Fiscal tab shows what yours changes. Each computer player leans toward a government that suits its civilization, so they spread across the systems.
Every civilization runs a mixed economy.
Government and ideology set each civilization's economic system.
A bit of everything: standard rates and credit, and the world's booms and slumps reach you at their usual strength.
Private capital and price signals: bonds cost 10 percent less and your economy recovers from a slump faster, but a Panic hits you harder.
You take wealth to pay for expansion: Heavy Taxation and War Levy bring more Gold, your aid buys twice the goodwill, and you borrow only from other civilizations, at 20 percent more.

Your citizens fund the state: you can borrow from them, and the interest comes back as celebration. Light Taxation celebrates more and Heavy Taxation costs more Happiness. Your Trade buildings move bills by 12 percent each and your Commerce buildings count a quarter more.
Finance runs the state: you borrow and lend at 20 percent less, your credit limit is 4 turns of income higher, and booms and slumps swing you harder, a Panic most of all.

Local stability over money: taxes come in kind, half the Gold and half the Happiness cost. You pay 20 percent less on trade bills, your warehouses shelter twice as much from a slump, the world's swings reach you less, and your credit limit is 4 turns lower.

You get rich exporting: you're owed 10 percent more on bills, a High tariff costs relationship half as often, bonds cost 20 percent less, your investments earn a point more, and booms and slumps swing you harder.
Interest is forbidden: what you lend comes back as a share that follows the borrower's income, and your aid buys twice the goodwill.

Capital goes to industry and war: War Levy pays its full wartime amount in peace too, a war booms your own economy and peace brings it down, your credit limit is half again as large and bonds cost 25 percent less, your prices climb twice as fast with inflation, your factories count twice for demand, and you take development loans only.

The treasury becomes production: a fifth of your Gold income goes into your cities' builds each turn, you buy at fixed prices, the world's booms and slumps pass you by, you borrow only from other civilizations and you take development loans only.
